utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. May we proceed immediately and please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Koumjian and case manager, Ruth Karper, appears with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Branko Lukic and Mr. John Ostojic accompanied by Mr. Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask the accused in person whether or not he is able to follow the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to apologise for what happened yesterday, although it was beyond my wishes, this problem that arose yesterday. I feel a bit better today. It is true that I still feel a little bit exhausted, but I do not feel often an urgent need to go to the bathroom. Once again, my apologies to the Court for yesterday, and thank you for understanding my situation yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And just in case there should arise a problem, please let us know immediately. And once again, a special good afternoon to you, Mr. Murselovic. And yes, the Prosecutor may start or proceed with the examination-in-chief, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Waidyaratne: [Continued].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, on Monday, when we concluded, you were describing the events in 1992 while you were detained in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were sometimes detained in the area called the pista.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were detained in that area or any other place, for instance, the Mujo's room, especially the pista, did you see a yellow-coloured truck coming into the camp?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I could see took place in the early afternoon hours. Usually, it would stop by the white house, the so-called white house, where bodies would lie. I was some 20 metres away from that spot, and those dead bodies just lay about the lawn. Usually, they would be loaded on to the truck when the truck arrived. The number varied from five, six, seven, to 12 or 13. Mostly it was in the morning that we would see these bodies, which would then subsequently be loaded on to this yellow small truck -- small yellow truck which had a cabin, driver's cabin in the front, and the back part was used to transport various cargo. And it was in this back area of the truck that the bodies would be loaded. The loading itself would last for about five or six minutes, after which the truck would leave. It would be gone for about 30 to 45 minutes, and then came back. So we concluded that the bodies were taken to a place in the vicinity. The truck would usually come back empty without the bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Murselovic, you spoke about dead bodies. Do you know as to who these people who were dead?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, the area was some 20, 25, maybe even 30 metres away from where I was, and it was not possible for me to recognise the bodies. However, I know several people who died in my group, in the so-called Mujo's room, who were taken out, whose bodies were taken out during the day. They would usually die inside, in the room where we were as a result of the beatings which they had undergone during the interrogation. And I saw a couple of such dead bodies in the room. Several people died in the room while we were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these were the bodies of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the bodies of the detainees, the civilians. We saw this truck, but we didn't see actually -- couldn't recognise the bodies, but one could tell that they were detainees, civilians, wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the person who drove or did you come to know the person who drove the truck?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never learned that. There was talk about his identity, but I don't remember who it was. Apparently, it was a former employee of the mines who drove this truck, but I didn't know him, nor did I know his name. I didn't try to learn his name, but I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Murselovic, going to another area, could you tell the Court, the Chamber, as to when you left the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sometime in early August 1992 after 60 or 65 days of detention, according to my calculations. Names were suddenly called out, and it was then that I was singled out together with a group of other people and put into a garage, which after some time we left. We could see that something was going on, but we didn't know what. The roll calls took place every day. There was the first group, the second group, and the third group of people. We didn't know what it all meant. And then it was either on the fifth or the sixth of August that the buses arrived, and my group, the one who were in the garage, was the first group to be called out. Other buses followed. And according to our estimates, there were at least ten or a dozen of such buses on to which we were subsequently loaded. The camp guards didn't tell us anything about where we were going. So we didn't know where we were off to. They all came to watch the whole process of putting us on the buses. I think that we were over a hundred in my bus. First, our names were read out, the names of the people from the first group, from the garage, some 150, 160 of us. We were called out first, and then another group of maybe 20 or 30 young men, civilians, were added. So there were over a hundred of people in each bus. So we set out that day on those buses. We were told to lie down on the floor. No one was allowed to sit on the bus seats, but we were made to lie down on the bus floor. We were not allowed to look up. We couldn't raise our heads. We could not see anything through the window of the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did the bus go to? Did you get to know as to where you all were taken to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some people managed to take a peep outside, and they felt that we were moving in the direction of Banja Luka. It lasted quite a while. I think that it was 9.00 or 10.00 in the morning when all of us were finally loaded on to the buses which didn't start for another hour maybe. And then they moved in the direction of Banja Luka. As we were lying down, we felt -- we realised that we were going towards Banja Luka. After all, we know the area very well. But we were crowded, lying on top of one another, lying on our stomachs, but in two -- how shall I put it -- layers. So as I said, we were moving along the road going towards Banja Luka. But at one point, we realised we had passed Banja Luka. It wasn't until later, 10.00 in the evening, that we realised that we -- where we were going. We thought that we might end at Manjaca, because it used to be an ex-JNA training ground. We were familiar with the spot, because before the war, in peacetime, we were often called up to do military exercises there. So we arrived there at about 10.00 or 11.00 in the evening. It was pitch dark. Throughout that period of time, the doors of the bus were tightly shut. The guards sat in the front. We were told to vacate the first two rows of the seats on the bus which made quite a few stops on the way. The guards would leave the bus, and then come back again. We were not able to look outside. We passed a number of villages, and we knew that a lot of people stopped or were standing by the road as the buses were passing through those villages. The people were shouting something, throwing things at us. It was a bus which belonged to the public transport company, and it had three doors. As we were lying down on our stomachs, the guards walked on our backs, and they verbally abused us all the time, telling us how we stank, how we balijas stank and various kinds of verbal abuse. They also made us sing Serb songs such as the famous one "Who is saying, who is lying, Serbia is small," and other Serbian nationalist songs. Before we left, they had given us some food which had gone bad, some kind of beans, I think. And many detainees had to go to the bathroom. They couldn't control themselves. They relieved themselves on the bus. And it was terrible. It was disgusting. The heating was on, and mind you, it was the 5th of August. So the heat was unbearable. I suffer from diabetes, and I wanted to get close to the window as often as I could to lick it a little bit because it was wet. I think it is, apart from those days that I spent in the garage, in the camp, I think that this was the worst day in my life, this transport to Manjaca. When we arrived at about 10.00 or 11.00, they didn't let us go out. They closed the doors of the bus. They let the heating on, and this is how we spent the night. The next day, at about 6.00 a.m., the situation, of course, was terrible. We were all dirty, stinking. There was no water. The heating was still on, and some people were taken out from the buses. For example, I think I mentioned this already, a very good acquaintance of mine was taken out of my bus, an elderly gentleman, Mr. Edo [as interpreted] Crnalic. He was taken off the bus, and as soon as he was out, they started beating him. But I believe I already told you that. After the beating, he was thrown back. His body -- dead body was thrown back into the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, as the transcript states the name of the person, Crnalic as Edo, is it Edo or Dedo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dedo, D-E-D-O. His real name is Dedo Crnalic. You see, this name is often a nickname in my country, and it usually refers to an elderly gentleman, but it also exists as a name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you recall any others who were taken out and beaten that day?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That night, an acquaintance of mine, Nezir Krak was taken off another bus, and there were some other people who were taken off some other buses. And the next morning when we got out, some people were killed, including a young man whose name now escapes me, a former neighbour of mine. He worked in the copying service of a local company. We called him by a nickname, Djuzin. He had a sister whose name was Djuza. I don't remember his family name. But anyway, we called him Djuzin. And one of the guards as we were lining up -- actually, several guards came up to him and started beating him and they beat him to death. He never made it -- he never made it to the Manjaca camp actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Nezir Krak also beaten and killed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was taken out that night just like Dedo and killed. I think that there were six, seven, or eight other people who were killed in the same way, the night we arrived in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct if I say this was at the entrance of the Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the entrance to the Manjaca camp, on a clearing where the buses were stationed during the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Manjaca? Is it correct if I say until the 14th of November, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes. It was on the 14th or the 15th that we were assisted by the international Red Cross. When I say "we," I refer to the oldest detainees, those who were born before 1951, that is, those who were over 42, 43 years of age at the time. This first convoy carrying detainees from the camp left on that day. It was escorted by the ICRC, though the guards were also with us, however, the conditions were more or less normal. This transport was much more humane. We sat normally on the bus seats, and we went through the town of Banja Luka, and then further via Gradiska, which at the time was the so-called UNPA zone. Nova Gradiska is situated in Croatia. And it was then that we were taken to Karlovac in Croatia. This transport took place on the 14th and the 15th of November 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, may I ask what serious injuries, if any, you suffered due to the detention in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I sustained injuries which I hope will not have a lasting mark on my health. My ribs were fractured, and at times, I feel pain Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there. And so far, I don't feel any other injuries. But even worse than the injuries was the humiliation we had to suffer, this inhuman attitude to us citizens. There were very many prominent citizens amongst us, very honest entrepreneurs, intellectuals, and the wounds in our souls are certainly more lasting than physical injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, may I also ask you whether you lost any property in Prijedor or any property of yours was damaged due to the conflict that took place in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like all other people from Prijedor, my property, too, was very much damaged. Much of my property was, in fact, devastated, destroyed. An entire building I owned, that I built, was destroyed. The damage was quite considerable. But it is immoral to speak about material damage when one has lost one's best friends and other people whom one knew as a child. And, as I was a fairly well-to-do person, it is immoral to speak about what I lost in terms of property. In the camp, I lost my very best friends, dozens of very good friends, my colleagues that I worked with at school, intellectuals which Prijedor was proud of. And this was a far greater damage as far as I was concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, finally, could you explain your present position or the post that you hold in the Prijedor municipality and how that you have come to that post?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, and as I have already said in my testimony, I was deputy of the Municipal Assembly as part of the multiparty system in 1990. Following that, during the first elections after the war in 1997, I was once again elected deputy. And I was appointed vice-president of the assembly. At the third local elections held in 2000, I was once again elected deputy and appointed as president of the Municipal Assembly with a very large majority of the votes, of both the Bosniak and the Serb deputies. Also, during the general elections in the year 2000, I was elected as member of parliament of the assembly of Republika Srpska, and I am there today also as representing the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor and in election unit one. Now, I have been living in Prijedor for a period of almost four years. I don't have any problems. Much has changed since. And I have permanent residence in Prijedor. I have not had to deal with provocations and unpleasant situations. We, who are engaged in having people return, we are trying to create normal conditions for all people in Prijedor, both for the Bosniaks, the Serbs, and the Croats. And today, I can say that there are no major problems. The only problems are problems of an economic nature. The economy is in a catastrophic situation, but security problems no longer exist. The presence of the international community is rather noticeable in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And lastly, Mr. Murselovic, you're a member of the Initiative Party still. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That small party ceased to exist. In 1996, 1997, I joined a party called the "Party for Bosnia and Herzegovina." In a way, the party is a fairly multiethnic one, and it is active on the whole territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I represent that party in the national assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That concludes the direct examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask the Defence to start immediately with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Murselovic. My name is Branko Lukic, and along with Mr. Ostojic, I am representing Dr. Stakic. You have given us -- the Prosecution exhaustive explanations, and we ask your assistance to help us in clarifying some points.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will do this to the best of my ability, if I am able to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will be faced with a problem, because we're speaking the same language, so I kindly ask you that once I have asked my question, that you make a break so that the interpreters can do their job. Thank you. On page 2 of your statement of January 2002, that is, of this year, this current year, paragraph 1 of the B/C/S version, page 1, paragraph 2 of the English version also, you said: "A few years ago, I gave a statement to the ICTY. And I would like to give additional information and explanations." Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your mind, what was not clear in your statement made on December 14th, 1997?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what was unclear then. I believe that I was asked to supplement some points because it was herein that I could be a witness when the accused was Mr. Kovacevic, might have been Mr. Kovacevic, and this is possibly the reason why they had me make the statement. In 1997, there was no special reason for this. Could you perhaps be more specific in asking questions?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, here is something specific. You were first arrested on May 23rd, 1992, Saturday evening. Were you asked about arms, weapons then?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I explained this in great detail, how the arrest took place. And at the time, as far as weapons were concerned, I had my service gun, which I had had before. And the two policemen were discussing whether to take the weapon away from me or not. And then we started walking, and I said: "There were no problems." They didn't ask me to come back. I went to the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On April -- on May 30th, 1992, you surrendered your arm to Ranko Vujasinovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he asked me to do so. I returned home. I'm not a person who likes arms. I only kept arms because I was a fairly well-to-do person, so I had to use it for protection. Well, they came down, waited for me, took away my gun and my license, and then gave that to Ranko Vujasinovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any shooting on that day in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the day Prijedor was attacked?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're referring to when you say "attacked." On April 30th, Prijedor was attacked. It was then that the SDS attacked Prijedor with arms and took over power. To my mind, this was an attack against the legal institutions, the legal authorities, and against the citizens and the entire town, to set up an abnormal state of affairs. And to my mind, this was the attack on Prijedor, but I must confess and say that on May 30th, there had been shooting. I didn't know what was going on. Later on, during subsequent events and talks, and the contacts I had -- during the contacts I had at the camp, I was told that there had been an attempt -- I don't know how to explain this -- of an organised -- organised by the Bosniaks and Croats to restore the situation in Prijedor to its previous state. I must say I cannot explain this. I think it was a very skillful, cunning attempt and ploy because in Prijedor at the time, there were huge quantities of heavy weapons in Prijedor, tanks. People were fully armed, and I don't see how a small group of people, however it may seem brave and silly, how they could attack a town which has at least a population of 50.000. I couldn't believe this. Truly it seemed very naive to me, if that had actually happened. I found out about it only later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you owned two restaurants, one restaurant, and one fast-food place.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Milomir Stakic occasionally visited your -- frequented your establishments?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from time to time. During the war events and the aftermath, I actually did see him with Rajic at my snack bar. But he did not come frequently. At least, I did not pay much attention to him. But I do remember, it is still vivid in my mind, I know where he and Mr. Cehajic stood, at the entrance on the left-hand side. They were standing and having breakfast. This was in the morning hours, and it was only natural because they worked together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Milomir Stakic know you were a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course he did. The names differ. One can tell by someone's name what ethnic background he is. Of course he knew I was a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 2, paragraph 4 of the B/C/S version of your statement, the same page, and I believe the same paragraph in the English version of your statement, you declared -- you stated the following: "I believe that Cehajic was involved in the work of the Executive Board more than what was the President of the assembly supposed to do, the reason being the fact that Kovacevic probably did not correctly fulfill his duties." Is this correct? Did you state that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. And my opinion has not changed since. I believe that in situations of various forms of obstruction, such as failure to attend meetings and sessions, failure to fulfill one's duties, the Executive Board, being a body in charge of preparing documents for the national assembly, because it's an executive body, but we believed -- we deputies believed that Dr. Kovacevic, the president of the Executive Board, had a very relaxed attitude towards his work. I received some reports, being a deputy to the assembly, to the effect that he failed to attend meetings of the Executive Board. And then Cehajic, being the most responsible official, to harmonise the work and to solve the problem, I think that he maybe didn't have to do that. I think that instead of doing that, instead of investing a lot of effort of his own, he should have tried to make Mr. Kovacevic do his job properly. But that was their business. However, it was something that we talked about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us some specific examples of the involvement of Cehajic in the work of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a member of the Executive Board myself. And in my capacity of an assembly deputy, although I could attend meetings of the Executive Board, I did not. And I didn't have to attend these meetings. So I don't know. However, it was the overall impression that Mr. Kovacevic was not sufficiently interested in the work he was supposed to do. This is what was talked about in the corridors of the assembly. I don't know what the official position was. I know that Mr. Cehajic wanted the assembly to function as best as it could. But this obstruction of the work of the assembly lasted for far too long. Sessions were not being held regularly, and it was Cehajic's desire, as the highly responsible official, the most responsible official, to have it function properly. To what extent he was able to make it happen, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the president of the Municipal Assembly? Did he have the right to perform the work and fulfill the duties of the president of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this type of situations, and in view of the overall structure of this service, the president of the Municipal Assembly was representative both of the legislative and the executive power. There is the mayor of the assembly, and the president of the Municipal Assembly. He was an embodiment, so to speak, of both legislative and executive power. He was superior to the overall municipal administration. Municipal administration was completely under his competence, so it was his, not only right, but his duty and obligation to monitor the work of the Executive Board because it was the Municipal Assembly that had elected the Executive Board. And the Executive Board was responsible and subordinate to the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be so kind and tell the Chamber and myself what particular regulation stipulates what you have just described?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was provided for by the then legislation, the appropriate provisions. There is a new law on the issue which is called the law on municipal administration today. However, it was not applicable at that time and the functions of the head of the municipality and the president of the Municipal Assembly were not clearly divided. This new law, which was promulgated in the year 2000, strictly divides the scope of duties of the legislative body and the executive body. In accordance with this new law, I am no longer the president of the municipality, the head of the municipality; I am the president of the Municipal Assembly, and there is another individual who is a head -- the head of the municipality. And he is in charge of the overall municipal administration. And he's in a position to employ and dismiss officials. And whatever used to be the province of -- this used to be the province of the president of the municipality before. Now, these two functions, these two offices, are strictly divided, which did not used to be the case. By enforcing these new provisions, I think we have come closer to the western model of local government. And I should like to add one more point: As the president of the municipality, I'm no longer in a superior position to anyone within the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. municipal administration. I have, as my subordinate bodies, various specific bodies that I am in charge of. As for the municipal administration, it has nothing to do with me. I am not in a superior position to any official of the municipal administration. And that is the major difference between now and then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us clear the matter further on. Was there a law on local government in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the name of this law was. However, as it is now, the law of local administration and local government, it did not exist at the time. Not in this shape and form.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The work of the Municipal Assembly, was it regulated by a statute, a statute of the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Of course, there was a statute and the rules of procedure of the assembly, Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this statute provide for what you have just explained, that the president of the municipality was superior to the municipal administration?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that that was the case. You're asking me something which was effected a long time before I became a member of the local government, but I know that he was superior to all of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Cehajic president of the municipality or president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall repeat it once again for you. He was the president of the municipality, the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, and also the president of the overall municipal administration, whereas today, these two offices are separate. Today there is the president of the assembly or parliament, local parliament. The word "assembly" usually refers to a collective body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The official name is the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. And I am, by my function, the president of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly. That is the name of the office that I hold now. I am a chief of the assembly, which consist of various political parties. They make decisions, and I chair their sessions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we, therefore, conclude, that Mr. Cehajic was also the president of the Municipal Assembly? Was that also the official title of his office, or was he the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was the president of the municipality. He was the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor and the municipality of Prijedor. That's what I'm trying to tell you. This was one and the same office at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please be so kind and tell me the name of his office?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of the municipality. No, I'm sorry, president of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We should have it quite clear, could you please repeat the answer. We have a problem with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cehajic was the president of the municipality. That is, the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. He was the president of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we agree that his duties and authority were stipulated in the statute of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor and described in the rules of procedure of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it possible for you, did it have the right to fulfill the duties, which were not envisaged as such by the statute and the rules of procedure of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you, he had the obligation of supervising the work of the municipal administration and its bodies. It was his responsibility. He was in charge of coordinating the work of various services within the municipality. I have already stated, but I will repeat that it was our opinion that Mr. Kovacevic should have engaged himself more, should have invested more effort in his work. That is what we discussed amongst us. But he certainly worked in accordance with the statute and the rules of procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On the same page, page 2, paragraph 6, you stated the following: "Today, 1992, [as interpreted] the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor is organised in a different way than it was the case in 1992." "Before the war, the assembly had both executive and legislative authority. At that time, the president of the assembly was also the head of the administration." Now, it means that the assembly had both executive and legislative authority. Are you aware of the fact that, in accordance with the laws of the former Yugoslavia, it was strictly forbidden for one particular body to be vested with both types of authority, the legislative and the executive authority, and that the laws of the former Yugoslavia expressly envisaged the three-fold nature of government, whereby it was divided in legislative, judicial, and executive government, that is the typical three-fold division of power?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you one thing: Everything was possible in the former Yugoslavia, in accordance with its laws. I know that the usual division of power is into legislative, executive, and judicial power in a typical western democracy. That is the case in my country today. But, before the relevant provisions were passed in the year 2002, before these elections and before various reports were made by the international organisations inside Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was the president of the municipality and the president of the Municipal Assembly. But the president of the municipality was responsible, both for the functioning of the municipal administration and was also in charge of presiding over the Municipal Assembly. That was the case before. However, today, we have the normal democratic division of power into the legislative power, the executive power, and the judicial power. But that, once again, was not the case prior to 2002. The president of the municipality also presided over the assembly and was in charge of the municipal administration. I think that this is common knowledge to those who are involved in this issue. It was a novelty which was introduced in 2002. Today, we have the office of the president of the Municipal Assembly, who is the representative of the legislative power. And we have the head of municipality, who represents the executive power and is the chief of the overall municipal administration. These two offices are strictly apart. Of course, we have the judiciary, which is the third component of the government, but that is a different matter. I believe that things are clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I, too, think that things are clear, Mr. Murselovic, but not -- but they are not as you are trying to describe them unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Questions and not comments at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Municipal Assembly, did it have executive authority prior to 1992, and was this power embodied in the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the case. But this Executive Board was representing the executive authority. What you're saying is true, but the president of the municipality was also the president of both the legislative and executive authority.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: First, slow down, please. In the interest of interpretation, we want to understand you in a language we understand. And please, do not overlap, as it was the case right now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind and tell us the name of the statutory document which provides for what you're telling us today, or is it the case that you don't know the title of this document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course this was all provided for in the statute and the rules of procedure of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The Municipal Assembly was responsible to whom or to which body for its work?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the Municipal Assembly responsible to anyone for its work?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Municipal Assembly is responsible, first of all, to the electorate. Its responsibility derives from the fact that they had been elected for this purpose, to pass on various laws, make amendments, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the Executive Board? Who was it responsible to? To the president of the Municipal Assembly or to the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was responsible both to the president of the assembly and the Municipal Assembly in general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that, according to you, also provided for in the statute of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that that was still the case, even today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I attempted to elicit an answer to that effect a moment ago. Could you perhaps now tell us at least one part of the executive authority which could be fulfilled by the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could, for example, dismiss employees of the municipality. He could make -- he could influence the overall organisation of the municipality, make changes, and he signed documents to that effect in his capacity as the president of the municipality. He was also able to -- he could control the overall functioning of the executive authority, because it was the municipality itself that had elected this executive authority. So, all these reports were submitted to the Municipal Assembly and its president.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Could the usher give the witness Exhibit Number D3, please. It's the statute of Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's a draft statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Draft statute. That's right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you show to the witness Article Number 40, 4-0.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murselovic, could you please read Article 40 of the statute.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 40: "The president of the Municipal Assembly shall represent the assembly. The president of the assembly shall convene and organise assembly sessions and preside over them. The president of the assembly may initiate debates on matters within the competence of the assembly. The president of the assembly shall submit proposals for general enactments and reports, information, analyses, and other documents addressed to the assembly to the working bodies of the assembly. The president shall hear the solemn declaration by the officials elected or appointed by the assembly, unless otherwise prescribed by the statute. The president of the assembly should perform other tasks as this defined by the statute."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see here or in any other place in the statute -- can you see that the president of the Municipal Assembly holds any executive power?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't see whether this is the official statute of the municipality of Prijedor. June 1991. Working document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would be a convenient time to have a break now so we give the witness a chance to go through the document, and that way he could find if there is any executive powers in the hands of the president of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Probably you can come back later, and the witness may have the right during the break to read -- I emphasise -- this draft statute. And may I make this proposal also, in the light that we all know that a document can be read only as a whole, and it doesn't make much sense to concentrate on one article only, and therefore it would make sense to go on to -- with other questions right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murselovic, can you turn to Article 53. We spoke about the responsibility of the Executive Board. Could you kindly read Article 53 to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The executive organ of the municipality shall be the executive committee. Within the framework of the rights and duties of the municipality, the executive committee shall be accountable to the Municipal Assembly for the proposing and implementation of policy, decisions, and other regulations and general enactments, as well as for the direction and coordination of the work of the municipal administration bodies and organisations. The executive committee shall exercise its rights and perform its duties on the basis, and in accordance with, the constitution, this statute, and the law."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it said anywhere that the president of the Executive Board is responsible to the president of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not specified here, but it is said that within the assembly, the Executive Board is formed, is formed within the assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your mind, the president of the Municipal Assembly, could he Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. decide independently on matters pertaining to the assembly of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not. That is why he had a vice-president. And in a way, that is why he was responsible to the assembly. Now, whether he could do these things on his own, I don't believe he could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For a decision of the Municipal Assembly, would it require a majority vote in the assembly for the decision to be accepted?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are some decisions that can be adopted on the basis of a two-thirds majority vote and a majority vote. All this has been specified in this statute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You, as president of the Municipal Assembly, do you have to sign a decision for which you voted against, if this is the decision of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a president, if the assembly adopt a decision on the basis of a majority vote, regardless of the -- my views, I have to sign such a document. If something is not contrary to law or contrary to the constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, you have the right to refuse to sign a decision adopted by the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In practice, this rarely happened. The decisions that are adopted by the assembly, well, I am duty-bund to sign such decisions. This is stipulated in the statute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was superior to the professional services of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, as far as the professional services, well, the president of the assembly was the superior body, as far as they were concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you read Articles 50 and 51 of the statute.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The assembly secretary shall assist the assembly president in the preparations and organisations of the assembly sessions. The assembly secretary shall be appointed for a period of four years and can be appointed for no more than two consecutive terms." I must say that the secretary is always responsible for the work of the assembly services, but the president and the -- that is today, the secretary is responsible to the president. The assembly services, well -- actually, the secretary holds administrative responsibility, but the assembly services are responsible to the president. The president signs all the decisions of the assembly. If you allow me -- well, you asked me about something. Can I read Article 56? "On the basis of a decision of the assembly, the work and the organisation of the Executive Board is set up." Which means the assembly organises the work of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we agree that this is not a matter dealt with by the president of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the assembly, in any case, he presides over the assembly, and he is the most responsible person. He signs all the documents relevant to organisation and the work of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many votes does the president of the assembly have?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only one vote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain this better? Well, you're not explaining it to us. With one vote, does he have the right to vote once or several times?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has the right to vote only once, the same as all the other deputies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How many persons are employed in the assembly services of the assembly, more or less?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately four to five persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the employment figure of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 150.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 2, paragraph 7, not of the statute, of your statement, you say: "Before 1992, the assembly did have a say in who was the chief of the local police."

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "But for its day-to-day working, it was primarily responsible to its own regional administration and hierarchy." Do you remember having said that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my opinion: The police was called a municipal secretariat for internal affairs, and it was called -- it was referred to as "SUP," "interior," "internal affair," secretariat for internal affairs, which means that it was a municipal body. That was the organisation then, although things tended to change. At that particular point in time, it was referred to as "SUP".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, SUP was part of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then how do you know explain this? You said it was one of the secretariats?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... We want to understand your comments, please. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your mind, what this SUP one of the secretariats of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, it was one of the secretariats of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the municipality had a regional administration. Is the term "municipality" broader than the term "region"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it has been written here, but I would like to clarify the point. The attitude towards the police, and between the municipality and the police frequently changed. Now, this body is referred to as "MUP," ministry of internal affairs of the interior. In that case, the ministry is responsible for the whole organisation of the police. If it is referred to as "SUP" that means that it is one of the secretariats of the Municipal Assembly. At the time the Municipal Assembly, in some way, appointed Mr. Hasan Talundzic as chief of the police, which means that the municipality appointed him chief of police of the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when this SUPs, the secretariats of the interior, when did they become MUPs, that is to say ministries of the interior?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when this happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we agree that this was in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when this happened, when the organisation was set up. I know that the head of the police was appointed in some way by the municipality in early 1990, when the elections took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the designation "SUP" was changed to "MUP," did anything change in terms of organisation of that service, or was it simply a matter of changing names?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that when the designations changed, I believe that the links with the ministry of the interior became stronger in terms of organisation and in terms of responsibility to the Ministry of the Interior. But in any case, they were responsible for the situation in the municipality, security matters, dismissing and employing workers. I don't know what exactly the organisation was within the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the organisation of the police?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But we use the term "MUP" then that associates -- it's an association of stronger links with the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the appellation "SUP" was changed to "MUP," did structural changes take place within that organisation? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, would it be a convenient time now? It's an hour and a half after we started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, it would be convenient now. But before we have the break, without going into any details, and of course I've got your point, I should invite you to ask only questions about the real knowledge of the witness and not to try to start a judicial examination of this witness, because we have to find facts and not grey theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness yesterday -- actually, the day before went in a length describing the organisational MUP and SUP. So I had to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I said I've got your point, but please insert limits.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have to challenge his view of this organisation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I was just going to ask for a time estimate from the Defence. We have another witness, and I doubt we're going to get to that witness this afternoon and I'd like to excuse him if counsel agrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This witness is pretty eloquent, and good speaker. He tries to describe a lot about every question, so I think if we proceed in this manner, that it will take the whole day to question this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think in the interest of the waiting witness, it would be better to excuse the witness as the Judges also have some questions. Then we will meet again at 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Before we start again, I really want to ask Mr. Murselovic and the Defence counsel first to take care that we can identify the answer on the computer before you start with the answer or the next question; otherwise, we can't hear your answer in the appropriate way, and we are really interested in both the questions and the entire answers. And to come back to the question mentioned before, the Defence may really take into account the distinction between an expert witness and a witness. And it's not -- there may be other possibilities to demonstrate what possibly is the intention of the Defence to make an expedition in the law of the municipality in theory and to point out possible discrepancies, possible developments. But a witness should be strictly only asked on questions on facts, but not on the law. Please understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm trying to quote his words. And afterwards, I'm -- all my questions follow from the parts -- either the parts of the statement of this witness, either from parts from yesterday's transcript -- of actually the day before yesterday. So I think that we have to clarify a few questions regarding the law which has been discussed by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murselovic, on page 2, paragraph 7 of the B/C/S version of your statement, page 2, paragraph 7 of the English version as well, of your statement given in 2002, you state as follows: "The assembly did have a say in who was the chief of the local police." Were you referring to the head of the public security station in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that as far as the three national parties are concerned, the SDS, SDA, and HDZ, that there was an interparty agreement on mutual establishment of government and the division of offices at various levels within the municipality? Were you aware of such an agreement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me remind you: The agreement in question envisaged that, at the municipal level, the party with the majority of votes will nominate its candidate for the president of the Municipal Assembly, and also, that it will nominate the candidate for the head of the public security station. Do you know that the SDA in Prijedor, that is, the Prijedor branch of the SDA, on the basis of this agreement, nominated Mr. Hasan Talundzic to the post of the chief of the public security station?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who eventually appointed Mr. Hasan Talundzic to the position of the public security station chief?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who it was who appointed him. It was 12 years ago. I am aware of such an agreement, and I know that the office in question was supposed to go to the Party for Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the minister of the Ministry of the Interior was the only authority who was able to appoint Mr. Hasan Talundzic to the post of the chief of public security station in Prijedor and signed a decision to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of this detail. It may be true. I believe it is true. However, at the local level, it was an interparty agreement that the post in question should go to the SDA, which means that consultations to that effect had been conducted at the municipality. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As regards the talks and negotiations concerning the division of power, were there any other participants apart from these three political associations? Were any other parties also involved?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were other political parties represented at the Prijedor Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were not. The three parties, the three main parties, the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ, which was a rather small party in this area, the Bosnian HDZ, because it got only two posts within the assembly. But it also participated to a certain degree in these agreements. So these three political parties had a total of 60 deputies and constituted a majority, so they were able to reach decisions to that effect. The remaining deputies had no say in the matter. And that is how it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the same page, page 2, in the last paragraph of the B/C/S version, you state as follows: "At one of the meetings, Cehajic -- I leave something out -- proposed that no police officer of Serb nationality should be dismissed but that Muslims should be appointed to their positions." Is that correct? Did you state this?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With your permission, I should like to elaborate the point. Mr. Cehajic, as the president of the municipality, spoke about a disproportionate ratio between the number of residents and the number of employees in the police service. He spoke about the statistical data regarding particular ethnic groups and to what extent their members participated in the police service. And he drew the attention to an obvious disproportion in the surrounding municipalities. He mentioned to that effect the municipality of Bosanski Novi, Bosanska Dubica, Prijedor, and so on and so forth. And he said that -- he showed us the data according to the last census in terms of ethnic background, and the number of employees in the police service. So this ratio was disproportionate. And Mr. Cehajic requested that the two should be brought closer together; that is, that a balance should be struck between the ethnic groups and the number of employees in the police force, which was perfectly understandable. And he said at the time that they did not ask for police officers of Serb nationality who constituted majority in the police service and outnumbered others and did not adequately reflect the number of Serbs living in the Prijedor municipality, that they should not be dismissed. However, that this disproportion should be taken into account so when new posts are made vacant, that the new coming police officers be Bosniaks or Croats so that an appropriate balance should be struck. So that was his proposal, which was opposed, and not only opposed but severely criticized, in the assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember when this particular session was held?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was sometime in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the Municipal Assembly is not competent to discuss these matters or to reach relevant decisions?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, the Municipal Assembly discussed the issue. I cannot agree with you when you say that Municipal Assembly cannot discuss the matter. It's a political issue. The Municipal Assembly has the right to discuss the position of a particular ethnic group if they believe that the said ethnic group is not sufficiently represented in the government. And it was perfectly normal for a Municipal Assembly, if they had nominated their person to the position of the chief of police, to remain involved in the matter. Because they nominated not only the chief of police, but his deputy and a number of other assistants. So their interest was perfectly natural. They did not want to see this disproportion that I just described. This was a very important area, because the chief of police was in charge of the security of the municipality, and it cooperated closely with the Municipal Assembly. It provided the Municipal Assembly with the information they needed and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time, was it an autonomous body?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by "autonomous"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the MUP responsible to anyone outside the usual chain of command and responsibility of the Ministry of the Interior? Was it responsible to anyone outside this ministry?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was the Municipal Assembly who appointed officials to leading positions, and you, yourself, pointed out that it was a political agreement, an interparty agreement, as to who should have these posts, of course then the Municipal Assembly had to know that an ethnic group -- the Municipal Assembly had to make sure that an ethnic group is adequately represented in the police force. But it is highly probable that as far as a hierarchy is concerned, it was the ministry of the republic, yes, the republic, the socialist republic at the time, coordinated -- and not only coordinated, but was superior to the secretariat of the interior in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will have to go back a little. I should like to know whether it was the political parties who proposed their candidates to the post of the public security station chief or was it the Municipal Assembly who nominated candidates?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you said, it was the political parties that were represented at the Municipal Assembly that made such proposals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this proposal submitted to the Prijedor Municipal Assembly, or to the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You spoke about an agreement and approval. We have to make an important distinction here. An "approval" is a formal act issued by a specific body. And an "agreement" is something different. The candidates are proposed by the local community. And, as you yourself have indicated, certain ministries today provide only their approval for a candidate. But the proposal itself, the nomination of the candidate itself, is agreed upon at the local level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said at the local level, between the political parties. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, at the local level between the parties who won the majority at the elections, and that was the case with the Prijedor municipality and its assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you making a distinction between proposals or nominations of candidates and the discussions as to who should be a candidate?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was able -- who could propose a candidate to a post?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ministry gives its approval -- the assembly gives its approval.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but who makes nominations? Who proposes candidates?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is the Municipal Assembly, but I'm not sure. When they agreed that the post should go to the Party of Democratic Action and the person in question was a Bosniak from Prijedor, it was an agreement. After the -- all of the candidates had been proposed, I think that we also gave our opinion on the candidate in question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 3 of your statement 2002, paragraph 1, you state as follows: "Talundzic couldn't do much because the majority of policemen who were his subordinates were of Serbian ethnic background and would not cooperate with him." Do you remember stating -- having stated this?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come you're aware of these problems?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was publicly discussed. People talked about the fact that Mr. Talundzic did not have any significant influence in what was going on within the police force. Before that, he had never been with the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this problem discussed at the Prijedor Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discuss this with Mr. Talundzic himself?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I used to meet with him quite often. And in these contacts with him, he would often complain that some of his subordinates did not obey him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, do you know who they were responsible to, outside their usual chain of command and their usual hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This was not part of my duties. They probably were responsible to the president, probably to the president of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So were they responsible to the government?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously. That is the case with all major systems in the world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who they reported to? Apart from the government, to whom they were responsible?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the Ministry of the Interior had their statutory provisions which stipulated their internal relationships, the rules of service, and command and control within the force?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I'm aware that such a document existed. The police force would not have been able to function without a document of the kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have an opportunity of reading any law, any regulations governing this particular issue?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 3, paragraph 2 of the B/C/S version, page 2, before-last paragraph of the English version, you stated the following: "I do not know who is responsible for appointing new police officers. And if the assembly had a role in that. I think the Prijedor public security station had the authority to higher junior officers." Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still maintain the same opinion. They were not imported from anywhere. There was a service that dealt with employing police officers, and these were all people who worked and lived in Prijedor. And they probably attended schools and got training and found employment in the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are not aware of the fact that in the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina, no one but the minister could sign a decision of employment, ranging from the cleaners up to the closest associates of the minister?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- are you aware of the fact that this rule is still in force in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even know that, but I think they have been divided in other organisational units, centres of public security. And Prijedor is no longer a centre of public security, but it's just a branch office. The Municipal Assembly has no jurisdiction over the police, but all this is connected with the centre of public security in Banja Luka. And there are five centres of this sort in the republic. So now what we have is a complete centralisation of this segment of public administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that in the federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, even today, the principle that was valid before the war still is valid today?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that, but I suppose the minister doesn't even know the people that are employed, regardless of the fact whether they are policemen or cleaners. It would be strange for him to choose and select these persons performing such lowly functions. The proposals usually come from the bottom, as we say, from a specific town, centre, secretariat. So it is not so important whether this will be signed by the minister because it is the question of a person working in the town. It is only a formality for the minister to sign such a notice because we have a centralisation in state administration. But as far as such lowly jobs, where they are concerned, local people probably made proposals and people were recruited from local communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour, at this time, take up an objection, although the witness has answered the question. The witness has clearly said that he does not know as to how these things are signed and so on. So I would place a request, Your Honour, to record my objection. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Indeed. It would be preferable for all of us if the Defence would restrict themselves to those points which can be of the knowledge of the witness. And we shouldn't go into guessing games.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honours, the Defence would be pleased with the answer "yes" or "no." And if the witness is ready to answer "I don't know," we would leave the field, the matter. But the witness is trying to give us all the time explanations which are not in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the beginning, the witness, if I remember correctly -- I may be wrong -- said I don't know. And then you insisted. But please, continue. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, did you take part in negotiations about the division of power?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Murselovic, you said that you were a deputy in the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, representing the Party of Private Initiative?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is the programme platform of your party, if you recollect them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these were, in fact -- this was a party rallying private businessmen, people in the restaurant business, shop owners, and public transport -- well, transport people, people who formed the party, people who were self-employed, who would in the forthcoming multiparty system protect the interests of its membership because we considered that we were best able, through the multiparty system and through participating in the work of the assembly, to protect our own interests. What does this imply, in fact, when we say "protecting our own interests"? Until then, under socialism, the prevailing form of ownership was state or what we called "social ownership." There were many regulations, contributions. Our status was, in fact, assessed, and the contributions and taxes usually greater than those paid by socially owned companies. We thought that by fighting for our status through the multiparty system, we would be best able to protect our interests. We were familiar with our own status, and we knew where we were jeopardised in the social and economic sense. And this, in fact, was the programme of our party because until 1990 in Prijedor, there were about 2000 self-employed entrepreneurs, and at least a thousand people who were employed by the self-employed entrepreneurs, and we targeted that category of people. We, in fact, represented small-time capital, and we wished to protect our interests because usually socially owned, state-owned, companies were predominant in all respects in terms -- there was a problem of taxes, that the taxes were higher. We had to pay higher taxes, and we were only allowed to employ a limited number of employees. It was only until after 1984 that we were able to employee more than five workers. We wished to take part in decisions and in that way protect the interests of private entrepreneurs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your party, did you view the market? Did you have in your programme a vision of a unified Yugoslav market, or did you have other views?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the party was organised on the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I don't remember all the details of our programme. Are you alluding to the market being a Yugoslav one? Nevertheless, I want to say that if you asked me personally, I, as a businessman, am more interested in a broader market. In my restaurant, I had guests coming from all parts of the former Yugoslavia, Serbia, Slovenia, Macedonia, and so on. And this is something which I believe that should exist today, economic space, a broader economic space, and this is how our economy in the former Yugoslavia developed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware, that is to say, in your programme, in the programme of your party, whether there were -- there was also the struggle for a unified Yugoslav market?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether this was included in our programme, but when the party was established in 1989, before the multiparty elections, no one even contemplated the possibility of Yugoslavia disappearing and not having a unified economic space.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see that you owned two restaurants. We see, we can say quite openly, that you were one of the wealthier citizens of Prijedor, that you were a well-respected and prominent member of the community before the war, and even today. You said that you had acquired your property through work and this was something that had been acquired through generations. Can you tell us whether there were other people similar to you in Prijedor? Can you recall their names?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were quite a few people who, like me, had property. And I could recollect the names of many people who had property.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you quote some of the names?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Senadin Ramadanovic, who owned a pastry shop. This was something also which had been set up through generation. Then another person who is a caterer, who had a large restaurant. His name was Niko Crnalic and there were other people who were engaged in other activities. There were the three brothers Kapetanovic. There was a caterer, Nedjo Delic was his name from Europe. He even has a restaurant today, and he is also one of the more prominent and well-to-do citizens of the town. Well, this was rather relative. It was not something that is tantamount to what one could term wealthy in the west. There were people who were sometimes more, sometimes less successful at their work. There was a caterer -- because I'm familiar with them. His name was Luka from Sanicani. He was a Croat. He had a fish restaurant. And there were other people of different ethnicities.
