Well, not very many of them have remained, at least of the Bosniaks. They have built this property through long years of effort. Some of them were employed abroad. They were employed in Germany, Austria. They brought capital to the country, and another person who came into that category was a person called Nedjo Delic who had his catering establishment, too. I was comparatively younger than most of these people. But my father, my late father, was employed in the area for over 50 years. And I, in fact, inherited this from him because I was the only son. This was my vocation, and I decided to engage in that activity as soon as I finished high school. This was quite unusual. I could have studied any other subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there prominent and well-respected in Prijedor who worked in state establishments like engineers and doctors?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But as you know, these engineers and educated people under socialism, they had socially owned apartments. They had a situation of security. And at the time, it was not possible to open up a private surgery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you mention some names?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can mention some of the physicians, of the doctors. Dr. Esad Sadikovic, who was a specialist, who was director of a hospital. Mahmuljin, Osman was another name. I'm just mentioning the people I knew, I was familiar with the educated set. There were many other people. There were many, as I said, doctors, professors. But they were generally employed in the social sector, and their status was reflected in the former socialist system. They had comfortable apartments. They didn't have much work to do. And very few, in fact, wished to engage in private business. Some of the activities, as I said, were not -- were not legal. A doctor could not open up a private surgery. A director could not open up a factory because you could employ only five people. And obviously these were people who had a much broader vision, broader horizons. These were basically craft shops which were opened which employed a very small number of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know names of well-known people who were engaged in politics under socialism?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I would like to mention the name of Miro Turnusek. He was president of the assembly for some time. He was also president of the committee for a mandate. And he was a good engineer, a technologist, a director of a large factory. And then Mira Cikota. It was a part of the Kras confectionery factory from Zagreb. He was a very well-respected person and he had excellent contacts with people from the former Yugoslav republics. He was a regular guest of mine. And unfortunately, as a Croat, he survived Manjaca and Omarska, and now he lives in Rijeka. Otherwise, he is married to a Serbian woman. He was pro-Yugoslav, in the true sense of word. He married a Serbian woman. He has a wonderful marriage. He has two children, and he now comes to visit Prijedor from time to time. Well, I know all the managers of companies, of the coal mines, of the other establishments there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement given in 1997, I don't see the number of the page, but it's 557, the ERN number, sixth paragraph; page 2 of the English version, sixth paragraph, you stated your opinion that the most influential politicians in Prijedor, the most important politicians in Prijedor were Simo Miskovic, the was the president of the SDS, Dragan Savanovic, who was the president of the club of SDS board members, and Srdjo Srdic, a deputy to the assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I mention anyone else?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you did, but you said that these three were the most powerful. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could I please ask the Defence to quote the entire paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The most important politicians were the following: Simo Miskovic, president of the SDS; Dragan Savanovic, president of the club of the SDS deputies; Srdjo Srdic, deputy to the BH assembly in Sarajevo; Milomir Stakic, vice-president of the Municipal Assembly; Kovacevic, president of the Executive Board. I consider the first three to be the most powerful politicians in Prijedor."

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you want to hear my comment --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to confirm that this is correct, that that is what you stated.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is indeed what I stated, and I still abide by m statement given at the time that these three were the most important. I failed to mention, for example, Mr. Timarac, who passed away in the meantime. He's from Omarska by origin. So, I didn't mention all of them. I didn't mention many other individuals. I spoke about those whom I saw daily. For instance, I was very surprised, surprised to hear that Srdjo Srdic was a very sociable person, who was a local amateur actor and singer. I also mentioned Mr. Miskovic whom I see regularly in Prijedor today. He was the president of this political party which means that he was its leader. I mentioned the president of the Executive Board. So it was in this context, that I mentioned Mr. -- Dr. Milomir Stakic. He was much younger than the rest. He had been elected to the office of the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly, and to be perfectly honest, I did not know him prior to 1990. But these are the individuals that I still consider to be very important participants in the work of the SDS, and that they were very responsible for whatever was going on within the SDS at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 580, third paragraph of the B/C/S version, or page 3, paragraph 4 of the English version of your statement, you say the following: "The Municipal Assembly had to decide the daily problems within the municipality. Decisions regarding issues in the regional or even republican level were not the assembly's competence." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, I would really ask, if there is a quote, to quote in the context. And evidently, the next sentence forms part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Do you want me to real the whole paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm now going to read the entire paragraph: "Sometime before the war, the Municipal Assembly was not able to function properly. The SDS was obstructing its work. The Municipal Assembly had to decide on daily problems in the municipality. Decisions regarding issues on the regional or even republican level were not in the competence of this assembly. However, the SDS requested the assembly to decide that BH should remain in the Republic of Yugoslavia. When this request was rejected, the entire group of the SDS assembly members left the assembly session. The president Cehajic then terminated the session, although the opposition parties tried to convince him to continue the meetings without the SDS. The local problems, therefore, could no longer be solved." Did you state this?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And I still abide by this statement of mine. I would again place my signature on it. It was a local Municipal Assembly. And attempts were made to have this local assembly reach a very important decision. The international -- the possibility of the international recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina was being discussed; and when this was discussed in the media, for example, together with many other issues, because in the meantime, some republics expressed a desire to secede from the former Yugoslavia. So when the talks at the level of the presidents Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the former republics were going on and were viewed by the general public as an endless journey between Belgrade, Ljubljana, Zagreb, and so on, so in view of the overall situation when one could see clearly that the entire Yugoslavia was severely under this pressure. To ask from a local assembly, to reach a decision on the Prijedor municipality and its remaining within the former Yugoslavia, this was simply ridiculous for us. Because of course this was not a decision that could have been reached by a very small municipality such as Prijedor. And when some of the deputies said that they were not willing to discuss the issue and they were not willing to vote on the issue because the issue was voted on, although more than half of the deputies stated that this was something that they could not vote on and could not discuss, then the Serb deputies left the assembly. Mr. Cehajic really did his best to have the assembly sessions going on and to have the assembly function properly, then put an end to this particular session, and he said: "We will close this session because as you can see, the Serb democratic party has walked out." And I remember that I got up, I took the floor, and I said: "Well, Mr. President, we have a quorum here. We can go on with the agenda of the session. We haven't started the agenda at all. We have a quorum and I think we can proceed with our usual work." There were almost 60 of us in the meeting called, so we were more than half. But then for reasons unknown to me, Cehajic adjourned the session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm afraid we have to go back once again to what we previously discussed; namely, Mr. Cehajic comparing the ratio of Bosniaks and Croats and Serbs within the police force. Was it possible for him to issue any orders to that effect? Could he order anything to be done?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that he could do anything. I think he acted in good faith. I think he saw it necessary for this balance to be struck in the near future.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Executive Board of the Prijedor municipality was eight members strong. It had its president, vice-president, and additional six members who were secretaries or heads of various departments.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Secretariats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The president of the Executive Board, could he issue orders to any of the secretaries or heads to do something? And let me give you a specific example: The president of the Executive Board, could he issue an order to the head of the land survey department to issue a construction permit to anyone? Or was it something that he could not interfere with? Was it the case that he could not interfere with the daily work of the various departments?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe these issues are specified in the statute. As the president of the Executive Board, he was the person who was in charge of coordinating the work of municipal secretariats, but that the decision itself would always eventually be reached by the secretary of the relevant department who would also sign a decision to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cehajic, as the president of the Municipal Assembly, could he order secretaries or heads of various departments? Could he issue orders to them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I still owe you a question from before the break. You refer me to this old statute, and I believe when citing specific articles, you failed to mention the general context. So, with your permission, I should like to read out some articles which I believe are very good illustration for the type of coordination between the president of the Municipal Assembly, the president of the Executive Board, and the various heads of secretariats or departments. Article 49: "The president of the Municipal Assembly -- the president of the Municipal Assembly shall, together with the vice-president of the assembly and the assembly secretary, consider issues of coordination and scheduling of the work of the assembly's working bodies, attend to the implementation of established policy and conclusions of the assembly, ensure cooperation of the assembly with organisations and communities with the assembly of the BH" and so on and so forth, "with the realisation of intermunicipal cooperation." "The chairman or the deputy chairman of the executive committee and other officials of the Municipal Assembly may, as the need arise, take part in the consideration of all issues." So this is not an issue. Let us see about the secretary of the assembly. You also asked about that. "The assembly secretary shall assist the assembly president in the preparations and organisations of the assembly sessions and perform other tasks prescribed in the statute or entrusted to him by the president of the assembly." So he is in a direct relationship of superiority with the assembly president. "The assembly secretary" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this was by way of introduction, as far as the municipal administration is concerned. You also asked me, and you put it to me in your question, that the president of the Municipal Assembly was not superior to the municipal administration, and I believe there was some misunderstanding regarding this issue. "And other administrative work" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please tell us which article he's reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's helpful for the transcript as well as for the interpreters if you quote the paragraph of the article you are just reading. And the document is in the hand of the booth? Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent. Article 60. Article 62, which provides as follows: "The assembly and the executive committee shall supervise the work of the municipal organs of administration and administrative organisations." Let us move on. Article 61: "Municipal organs of administration and administrative organisations shall perform their duties independently and shall be accountable for their work to the assembly and the executive committee." Article 62, a very important point, once again: "The supervision over the work of the municipal organs of administration and administrative organisations, as provided for in Article 62, it is the assembly and the Executive Board who supervise the work of these organs." Article 63: "For the performance of administrative and other tasks in the sphere of the rights and duties of the municipality, a secretariat for administration shall be set up as an individual organ which performs administration and specialist tasks," and so on and so forth. Second paragraph: "Alternatively, in those municipalities where so required by the large amount of administrative work, municipal secretariats and municipal administrations may be established as individual organs of administration for the performance of administrative and other specialist tasks in one or more areas of administration." And there was one more thing that I wanted to tell you about, and that is the fact that the Municipal Assembly supervised the work of all bodies in question. And this supervision was shared with the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You read out a number of articles from the statute. Have you found in any of these provisions that the president of the Municipal Assembly had specific duties and competences, or was it the case that it was only the Municipal Assembly which was vested with these competences?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you something about the secretary: The secretary is responsible for his work to the municipal -- Article 50: "The assembly secretary shall assist the assembly president in the preparations and organisations of the assembly sessions and perform other tasks pursuant to the statute or entrusted to him by the president. The assembly supervises the work and the president is, of course, the president of the assembly."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In respect of whom we have established --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please don't overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- he has only one vote as is the case with other deputies?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Municipal Assembly, does it employ individuals who are directly responsible to the government - at the time, it was the government of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina - such as a number of inspection departments, as the administration for land survey and similar bodies?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The body in question, it is true, was directly linked to the municipality as a municipal secretariat for land survey and property relations. We called it simply a cadastre. It was a body which was one of the secretariats of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly. It was - well - independent, and the head or rather the secretary of this secretariat was appointed by the assembly. So he was responsible to the assembly. But I'm sure that it must have been a vertical chain of responsibility which made him also responsible to the relevant ministry or some other similar body at the level of the republic. Now, in Republika Srpska, we have a so-called direction for property relations and land survey. So a similar body exists in Prijedor still today. Some of its work is done for the municipality, but they do not have a direct relationship with the municipality. It is a rather unusual relationship, it is true, and attempts are now being made to have it back within the competence of the Municipal Assembly. And if I may add, it is an attempt to centralise and disempower the Municipal Assembly. I'm talking about the situation as it is nowadays.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as this land survey service is concerned, you think that that was not the case in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from local companies situated in the Prijedor municipality, there was a number of enterprises and public institutions, such as a branch of the public health fund, a branch of the public fund for pensions, a branch of the public fund for employment, a local social accountancy service, a PTT company, power distribution company, a company which was in charge of road maintenance and public communications, a branch of the Yugoslav railways company, and a number of other such companies. Are you aware of the existence of these institutions and organisations in the territory of the Prijedor municipality at the time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether these companies were financed by -- from the municipal budget or from some other source?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The railways had their own source of financing; the PTT, also the employment institutions, too. So these companies and institutions mostly were not financed from the municipal budget.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us to whom the managers of these companies and the heads of these institutions were responsible? To the Municipal Assembly? To any particular secretariat? Or to any republican body? Or to their founder, such as the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this entire sector concerning both economic and public institutions, they were state institutions, state entities, and they closely coordinated their work with the Municipal Assembly. Whether they were all financed from their budget or not is a matter of not much significance. However, these organisations, such as the employment bureau, were obliged to submit the relevant data, such as the number of unemployed and the break up per month concerning employment, they were required to submit these reports to the Executive Board. And the Executive Board then informed the Municipal Assembly of that. Some of these entities such as the power distribution company, in terms of organisation, they were sometimes linked with the municipality. There was a company called Elektrodistribucija Prijedor. It used to be called Elektrodistribucija Banja Luka which had its branch in Prijedor. But at any rate, the coordination or cooperation between all these public or state institutions were done by the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those organisations and institutions had to submit reports to the Executive Board. Did the Executive Board have any influence on the election of their officials? Was it able to revoke them from office, recall them from office?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if they could recall them. But you must know that in a one-party system, all this was, in a sense, directed by the League of Communists and the highest state bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did we have a one-party system in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't have a one-party system then. And you are asking me about a period when nothing really functioned. You are asking me how that functioned in such a set up. In 1991, I can say quite honestly that nothing functioned, that there were obstructions all over the place, and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it was -- everything just did not function.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am only trying to get an answer from you about whether you are aware of the laws and what the situation in practice was in respect of responsibility of people who headed such bodies. Who was there to appoint them? If you are not sure or if you do not know, we will move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must add something: Some organisations like the centre for social work, kindergartens, the press, well, now they are organised differently. And some of them are still linked up with the municipality, and appointment and agreements and reports, they are submitted to the municipality, if these were founded by the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's appropriate to have a break now. We resume at 6.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Before we restart, may I ask both Defence counsel and the witness to concentrate on the core issues of our case, that we at least can try to finalise the cross-examination at 7.00 sharp. The attempt should be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll try my best, Your Honour, but I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I ask both of you to be -- to concentrate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because right now, I've finalized only half of my questions. The same line of questions I finished with the other witness for less than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Bench doesn't regard it as a real threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you aware that the system of armed forces of the SFRY made up of the JNA, the Territorial Defence, the MUP, and the civil protection was regulated by a single federal law about general national defence?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the Territorial Defence units in case of immediate threat of war were subordinated and joined the units of the JNA, that is to say, they became a component part of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in addition to the municipal staffs of the TO, there were also regional and republic staffs of the TO?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had some knowledge about that, that there was a TO comprising the municipal Territorial Defence units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, for example, that the commander of a civil protection staff was responsible to the president of the assembly or the commander of the republic headquarters of civil defence?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The commander of the barracks in Prijedor, was he responsible to the municipality for his work, or according to the command line, was he responsible to the competent bodies of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose he was subordinated to the JNA, but whatever happened in Prijedor in spring of 1992 showed that both the municipality, the TO, and the JNA were strictly coordinating their efforts, work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 19, line 22 of the transcript of Monday, you said: "During the second half of 1991, the war in Croatia was in full swing. The Serb soldiers from Prijedor went to fight there. They were mobilised by the municipality of Prijedor to go to Croatia and to fight there." Who was president of the Municipal Assembly then?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cehajic was president of the assembly, but he publicly specified that it was not necessary for the Croats and Bosniaks to be mobilised and to fight the war on the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Muhamed Cehajic call the mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think there may be a mistake in the translation. He may have said yes. I will ask the question again. Was Mr. Muhamed Cehajic, was he the one to call the mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Muhamed Cehajic didn't do that. He was exclusively against fighting a war on the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that at a protest meeting in Prijedor, Mr. Medunjanin stated that the mobilisation was called on the level of the republic, and that people whistled when they heard that at the protest meeting?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. The only thing I know was that Mr. Cehajic and Mr. Medunjanin were not in favour of neither the Bosniaks or anyone else, to go to a territory and attack Croatia because there was such a propaganda going on at the time, in the press. It was shown that the civilians were being attacked, people rejoiced when houses were hit, and films and photographs were in the same vein. And there were similar reports from -- reporting from Croatia. And I, myself, and the vast majority of Bosniaks, Muslims, and Croatians and all of the citizens, decent citizens, were not in favour of going to Croatia and to target civilian buildings and to attack civilians. This was seen in the Kozarski Vjesnik and on many video films and the journalists and those who were on tanks, they were discussing which home to shoot, and they said, "Well, this house was, in fact, destroyed." And any normal person would be against this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know what Mr. Medunjanin's function was at the time, what post he occupied? Was he in the secretariat for national defence?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was secretary of the secretariat for national defence and social self-protection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the municipal secretariat?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Medunjanin call the mobilisation, or was this done on the level of the republic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that he called a written mobilisation. I don't know who actually did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the competence of the municipal secretariat for national defence was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipal secretariat, on the territory of a municipality, keeps records about able-bodied young men who are able to serve the army. It keeps records of them; it cooperates closely with the JNA. This is how it was organised at the time. It sends people -- in coordination with the army, it sends these people to serve their regular military service. It has in its possession lists of persons, of soldiers, that have already completed their military service. And then, after some time, and if the need arises, it sends these people on exercises as part of the reserve units. Exercises, we called this -- in fact, it was a question of keeping these people in shape and checking up on their shape. That body, in other words, keeps records about people -- young people who still have to serve the army; and following that, they also keep records of those who have completed their military service, and they have information as to where these people -- what units they served in, and then uses these people on different occasions to take part in different exercises if the need arises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who is competent to call a mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It was already now the third time you asked the same question, and the third time the witness answered "I don't know." I think it's enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the Municipal Assembly call a mobilisation or prevent this from happening?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, may I explain that the situation at the time was rather confused. And, as far as I was concerned, it was hard to imagine that people should go and fight a war in the republic of Croatia. And all the while, to write and speak about the horrors happening there and how civilian targets are being brought down and how the civilian population was being attacked. The first time I heard the expression that "soldiers were going to clean up the terrain," and if I were younger, I would also not like to have played a part in all of this and brought harm to my former neighbours. Armed people in the wings of the Yugoslav National Army on behalf of Yugoslavia. And when we speak of the breakup of Yugoslavia and the confused situation ensuing from that, to go to Croatia, I myself would not take part in such a war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Muhamed Cehajic as president of the Municipal Assembly and president of the council for national defence, was he able to order to the units of the JNA to abandon the territory of the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think so. All I know is that he stated publicly that the Bosniaks, Muslims, and Croats should not go to fight a war in Croatia. And I believe that was the right attitude, that he was right in saying that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Muhamed Cehajic, as president of the Municipal Assembly and president of the council for national defence, was he a subordinate -- superior body to issue orders to Arsic about the deployment of troops?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Cehajic, as president of the national defence council and of the assembly, was he able to appoint anyone from the army?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's very clear from the many answers of this witness that he answered very clearly that he was unaware as to what Mr. Muhamed Cehajic's position was, and that he was not aware of what took place. So therefore, I object to this line of questioning by my learned colleague. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 3 of your statement of 1997, you stated: "After the takeover of the municipality, a curfew was introduced. It was from 10.00 p.m. to some time in the morning. I cannot say if it was restricted to non-Serbs only, because I did not go out in the evening." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true that as soon as power -- after the takeover, the Crisis Staff declared a curfew which lasted from about -- from exactly 10.00 p.m. to some time in the morning, whether it was 5.00 or 6.00 -- I think it was 6.00 a.m. in the morning. And during that period, I didn't move around, and I'm not aware of the Bosniaks or any one of the Bosniaks or Croats moving around if they had no connections with the police or the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 4 of your statement of 1997, in paragraph 5, you said: "After the takeover, the situation in the town was very tense. Soldiers were returning from the front in Croatia. There was much propaganda on the radio. I cannot say that the propaganda was directly aimed at the non-Serbs, but the SDA proclaimed that Muslims did not fight against the Ustasha." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, generally, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there only one Crisis Staff in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there was only one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the Crisis Staff had issued an ultimatum about the killings in Hambarine. Do you remember that text, the text of the ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was stated that, following the incident that happened in Hambarine, I think it was on May 21st or 22nd, the second half of May, shooting occurred at the checkpoint in Hambarine. It is a Bosniak village. A whole enclave in which over 10.000 Bosniaks lived before the war, about 12.000 together with the Croatians. An incident took place when the drunk Serb soldiers passed by the checkpoint in Hambarine; and at one point, one or two soldiers were killed. They were in a vehicle. And how fire was opened and how they returned fire, well, I cannot remember all those details after a period of ten years and more. But what I can safely say, that the Crisis Staff reacted to this as it reacted to many events taking place in Prijedor. And they came up with a statement, that the culprits should surrender, a name was mentioned: Aziz Aliskovic. I think that was his name, who allegedly was the commander, or a Bosniak commander in Hambarine. I personally do not know him. And the Crisis Staff ordered, and this was reflected in the press and broadcast on the radio, it was repeated on many occasions that the culprits from amongst the Bosniaks should surrender.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware of the existence of a Hambarine Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard of that. All I know was that there was a handful of TO members there at Hambarine who were sort of guarding their houses, their village. Actually, I don't know what kind of organisation they belonged to, how they were organised. But it was a form of civil protection, civil defence, which was self-organised; that is, organised by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the local villagers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many members were with this defence?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the existence of a Crisis Staff which belonged to the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard that the SDA had a Crisis Staff of their own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't hear about the Crisis Staffs which were organised in local companies?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether companies had their own Crisis Staffs. However, every public company, state-owned company, had a segment which was in charge of civil defence or civil protection, all people's defence -- I don't know what it was officially called -- consisting of people who were supposed to provide protection to the company itself. But in those days, as this was going on, local companies no longer had any Croat or Bosniak employees, so these people were not working as of the 30th of April; that is, as of the takeover. Bosniaks and Croats no longer went to work, and they no longer participated in these type of activities. So I don't know what kind of Crisis Staffs would have been organised in local companies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were only leaders, leading officials, dismissed from these companies, or only -- or all other Bosniaks and Croats after the attack on Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the leaders who got sacked first. Immediately after the takeover by the Crisis Staff --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about other employees? Did they work until -- up until the conflict in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they were sent home from work. If any of them remained at work, I am sure that in the course of the month of May, they were turned back from work. All of them were actually turned back. I know that they were required to show their IDs and were sent home. I was there until the 30th of May, and I heard a lot of people complain of the fact that they were no longer denied access to their workplace. But many of them still went to work. It was a period of great confusion. However, a great majority was sent home and were banned from their companies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the existence of a Crisis Staff at the level of the republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as early as in the spring of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I don't know that there was a Crisis Staff of that name at the level of the republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I know that there was a republic organisation of the Territorial Defence. There were no organised armed forces in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time apart from the Territorial Defence and civil protection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The principle of the so-called constitutional character of people's is still -- is again topical in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Are you familiar with this issue?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very much so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This principle of constitutionality, was it applicable before the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes; however, it was not referred to in those terms. I remember a statement issued by the cabinet of the communist league of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the effect that Bosnia and Herzegovina was not a Croat, Serb, or Muslim entity, but it was all of the three at the same time. The idea being to show that all ethnic groups were equal. As for the idea of constitutionality, that is, of the constituent character of peoples, which in part has lately been imposed by the high representative, but has also been, to a certain extent, promulgated by the government, all constituent peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina are equal in their rights. It means that they have the constituent character as an ethnic group throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina which is provided for in the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was not the case previously with the entities. And I consider the development to be a very positive and significant for the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that as far as the 22nd of May attack on Hambarine was preceded by the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 19th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date of the withdrawal of the Yugoslav army from Bosnia and Herzegovina. They simply surrendered their weapons to the Serb community, to the members of the Serb ethnic group who were members of the JNA. So they were given their weapons. And before the war, before my detention in the camp, I identified this JNA with the Serb army. As to what happened on the 19th, as you said, I don't know whether this withdrawal took place on the 19th or a week later or before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the Muslims, or rather Bosniaks and Croats who responded to the mobilisation, callup? Were they sent to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must tell you that a very small number of people responded to callup papers and went to fight the war in Croatia. Really, an insignificant number. I don't think it would have been more than 1 or 2 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they given any weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They probably were. I don't know what kind of status they had there. But I know that quite a few of those who initially participated in the Serb army under arms were soon removed so that the number decreased even further. But I'm unable to tell you how many there were. There is another thing that I wish to add: A great majority of these people, that is Croats and Bosniaks who participated -- who were members of the Serb army, were eventually evicted and ethnically cleansed, both them and their families, from Prijedor, especially in 1995, when out of over 60.000 Croats and Bosniaks in Prijedor prior to the war, only a thousand and even less than a thousand remained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Prijedor -- that people left Prijedor in Santurs and Autoprevoz transport companies and went to Croatia before the outbreak of the war, went to Europe via Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Serbs took over power on the 30th of April and when people began feeling insecure because of the daily shooting incidents which were becoming ever more frequent, people were afraid. They were especially afraid for their women and children, so they started leaving the town in bus convoys. However, it was already impossible to leave the town. I think that over 90 per cent of the people left via Banja Luka, and eventually reached Belgrade and found planes there to leave the country. People were afraid for their future, especially those who had children and wives. But even before that, some people left because they were feeling increasingly insecure. But I must tell you, those times were, generally speaking, insecure. Throughout the night, for example, especially when soldiers came back from the front in Croatia, they were constantly intimidating people. They frequently opened fire, and the streets were littered with empty cartridges, especially at the approaches to the town. A number of incidents took place: People were taken off the local buses and killed. Many of such incidents were never elucidated. So this all instilled fear amongst the population. Serbs tried to justify it, and the Crisis Staff often publicly spoke after such incidents. But what they said was that it was necessary to protect the Serb population, that it was necessary to, sort of, prevent Serbs from reacting, from responding, to the attacks on them. The times, as I said, generally speaking were just insecure. The Prijedor-Bosanska Dubica Road was also often prone to such incidents. On one such occasion several people were taken off a bus and killed. A famous entrepreneur by the name of Kuckovic was taken off his vehicle and killed. So generally speaking, the Croat and Bosniak population was being intimidated all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 16, line 4 of the transcript of your testimony, you stated, when describing the president of the Municipal Assembly -- this is something that you repeated today -- this person could employ and dismiss officials. Could you refer us to the relevant provision? Where does it say so?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was the case in practice. The president of the Municipal Assembly was the person who signed decisions to that effect, who employed new officials. And as you just indicated -- actually, you're constantly trying to say that at that time, the president of the municipality did not constitute executive authority. And now you're saying that he not have the right to do what I just said, that you repeated. However, a moment ago, you said that the president of the municipality in these unusual circumstances also became a president of some kind of body which would have been in charge of the overall situation in Prijedor. I don't know exactly what you called it. Would you please refresh my memory. The president of the municipality, what exactly did he become before May 1992? What did you say he was?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The president of the Municipal Assembly is always the president of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you said that he, at that time, had taken up a function of some sort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the same page, you said: "He was also in charge of the budget, of the budget proposals, and of approving the budget." Can you refer me to the relevant provision for this particular issue?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was provided for in the relevant regulations of the Municipal Assembly. What I wanted to say was that both the approval of the budget and the responsibility for the implementation of the budget lay with the president of the municipality, which is not the case today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But at any rate, this particular issue is provided for in the relevant regulations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that he approves the budget.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 25, line 15 of the transcript of your testimony, you say: "Once the authority had been -- once the power had been taken over, the post of the president of the Crisis Staff was earmarked for Milomir Stakic." On page 27, line 17, you stated: "Milomir Stakic was the president of the Crisis Staff; at the same time, he was the president of the municipality." Did Milomir Stakic hold both of these positions at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already indicated during my testimony here, Mr. Milomir Stakic, before the decision on the establishment of the Serb municipality of Prijedor was reached sometime in February 1992, was the vice-president of the assembly. On that session, which I did not attend, but I presume it was the deputies of the Serb democratic party who reached a decision that a parallel kind of government should be established which they termed, which they called, "the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor." This was done publicly and announced in the media. And, as it was said, Milomir Stakic was the president of the assembly of this municipality. It was also stated at the time that Dr. Kovacevic was the president of the Executive Board, which he was actually, that the president of the Court was so and so. Anyway, all of these functions, all of these offices, which at the time were held by Serbs, remained the same. Changes concerned, of course, those offices which were headed by Muslims, Bosniaks, or Croats. And this Serbian municipality of Prijedor, as far as I'm concerned, was a ridiculous type of institution. It was really very funny to me at the time. And, up until the takeover on the 30th of April, this whole idea was, so to speak, dormant. But when this happened, the SDS, together with the army, because all of these people were armed, took over power on the 30th of April. And Milomir Stakic became president of the Crisis Staff and the president of the assembly. And he was physically in the office of the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. I told you I went over there to see for myself, because I found it all very unclear and confusing. I know that the SDS and the SDA shared power; but they could no longer bear to watch the SDS being involved in all that, and that is why they took over power, which normally was shared by them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please answer my question, now. Do you know and how is it that you know that Milomir Stakic was at the same time the president of the municipality and president of the Crisis Staff? How is it that you know that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the author of many public communiques which were broadcast in the media. There are documents to that effect. I'm telling you that Mr. Stakic was president of the Crisis Staff and that he was physically located in the office of the president of the Municipal Assembly, and this is where I saw him; this is where I talked to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor held a session on the 16th of May and the 20th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, when Serbs took over power, the assembly no longer sat. I think I would have known that, as its deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The interpreters missed your last question Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. because of the overlapping. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the Serbian Municipal Assembly of Prijedor met on the 16th and the 20th of May?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor did not meet in session because I, as its deputy, should have known that. Whether the Serbian assembly met in session, now that is something that I don't know. I never expressed any interest in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honours, I need at least half an hour to finish my cross-examination. I tried to speed up. I really quit at least two thirds of the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think then it's more favourable to proceed tomorrow, because there might be some re-examination, and there are numerous questions to be forwarded to our witness of today, which apparently is of utmost interest for both parties. And so please understand that we ask for your assistance also tomorrow. There will be a deadline for the cross-examination to be announced tomorrow. Therefore, I would ask you already today when preparing for the rest of the cross-examination, to concentrate on the most important questions and to avoid, first of all, repetitions. And there was another point?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just scheduling. I wanted the Trial Chamber to be aware that there are two witnesses here now. I think the next witness will take about -- I'm guessing -- one session, one full day, including cross-examination and the questions from the Bench. Normally, we would -- I know that the schedule is that we would not sit on Friday. Normally we would try to send the witness back to where the witness comes from, but apparently that's not possible. I just want to let the Court know that. So we're stacked up with -- perhaps we were overly optimistic with the three witnesses this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Unfortunately on Friday, there's no courtroom available. And then we have to proceed tomorrow. I think it will take us at least one and a half hour, and then hopefully we can proceed with the other witness. And I don't know whether you already succeeded or started on the question of agreed facts. Having reconsidered the questions of today, I would say we could have saved a good part of the time if we would have some agreed facts, because we wouldn't need the one or the other question from both sides. Though I wonder if it's possible to report to the legal officer of the Trial Chamber in how far you came to results on agreed facts. So we adjourn for today and resume tomorrow as scheduled, 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
